t: for the verse converted it into a positive commandment, that if he robbed he must return. The negative commandment ("you shall not rob") was converted into a positive commandment ("and he shall return the robbed item"), and one does not receive lashes for such a negative commandment (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).

and even if he burned the robbed item he does not receive lashes, etc.. Although for a negative commandment converted into a positive one, if he did not fulfill the positive commandment he receives lashes, and he should have received lashes since he did not return the robbed item, he is nonetheless exempt from lashes for another reason: since he must pay the value of the robbed item, and no negative commandment that carries a payment obligation incurs lashes (there, and see also Hilchot Genevah 1:1).
and it is forbidden to rob anything by Torah law. By the Torah it is forbidden to rob even less than the value of a perutah (except that there is no obligation to return it, as below 5:6).
even a gentile who serves idolatry it is forbidden to rob. See also Hilchot Genevah 1:1.
for example, that he snatched movable property from his hand. And with robbing land too he transgresses a negative commandment (Hilchot Genevah 7:11).
or that he overpowered his slaves and his animals. Seized them by force.
and used them. See below 3:6-7.
or that he went down into his field and ate its fruit. See below 9:5.
with the owners' consent. Unlike robbery, where the item came into his hand without the owners' consent.
for example, he had a loan or a deposit in his fellow's hand. That he lent to his fellow or deposited with him.

or wages. It seems this means that his fellow worked for him as a hired worker and he holds his wages in his hand and does not give them to him. And although in this case the fellow did not give him money, it is still included in the prohibition of oppression (see Sefer HaMitzvot, Negative Commandment 238, Hilchot Sechirut 11:2).
violent and hard. A violent person with whom it is hard to litigate.

the Sages enacted for the sake of the repentant that he give its value and not lose the building. They made an enactment to ease matters for robbers who wish to repent, since if returning the robbed item itself would cause a loss, it would make it hard for robbers to return to the right path (and see below halachah 13 and below 2:2 for further enactments to ease matters for the repentant).
and made it into the roof of a sukkah for the festival. He built it into the sukkah of the festival of Sukkot (see also Hilchot Sukkah 5:25).

he gives him its value. Since he fulfills a commandment with it, it is treated as a permanent building into which the enactment for the repentant applies on the festival, even though in itself it is not a permanent structure (Rashi and Meiri, Sukkah 31a).
but after the festival. If he claimed it from him after Sukkot.
and did not build it with mortar. For if he joined it with mortar it is judged a permanent structure and has the law of a beam built into a building (Rashi there).
it changed, he pays its value. As explained below chapter 2.

he must pay only the principal. Unlike a thief, who pays a fine if there are witnesses that he stole (Hilchot Genevah 1:4-6). And if he swore falsely and then admitted, he pays principal plus a fifth and brings a guilt offering (below 7:1-2).
and built it into the palace. Made it part of the palace, which is a large building.
since it did not change. Although now it is part of the building, nonetheless in itself it remains as it was.
even though he transgressed. The Torah prohibition of robbery.
it is not in the category of returning a robbed item. There is no commandment to return the robbed item.
bundles. Of vegetables and the like.
and the three of them are together worth two perutot and he returned two to him. So it turns out that he now holds a bundle worth less than a perutah.

there is robbery here but no commandment to return a robbed item here. He robbed the value of a perutah and became obligated to return it, but since less than a perutah of what he robbed remains in his hand, he is not obligated by the commandment of returning (the version before us in the Talmud, Bava Kamma 105a, reads: "there is no robbery here, and there is no commandment to return a robbed item here," and the Rishonim there brought several explanations; see the commentators who discussed the relationship between Maimonides' words here and this version).
in a settled place. An inhabited place.
lest it be seized from me here. For the wilderness is a place of danger and the robbed item is not safe with him.

and likewise with the value of the robbed item. In a case where he pays its value, the choice is the victim's not to receive the payment in the wilderness (see also Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 13:8, Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 7:11).
and slipped it to him in the account. When he settled accounts with the victim about another matter, he added the value of the robbed item into the account without his knowledge.

for a person tends to feel his purse at all times, etc.. A person is accustomed to check often how much money he has in his wallet, and one can assume that he already counted the coins that returned to him together with the other coins he had in his wallet.

and a count without knowledge discharges. Although the robber did not inform the owner that he had returned the money to his wallet, since the owner now knows that he has all his money, the robber is released from responsibility (compare Hilchot Genevah 4:10-11).

and if he returned it to a purse with nothing in it, he has not discharged. For he does not usually feel it at all times, and since he does not know that there is now money in it, he will not be careful to guard it.
and pressed him with friends and urged him until he took it from him. He sent his friends to persuade him to sell it to him until he finally agreed.
and one does not receive lashes for this negative commandment, for it involves no act. Since the prohibition is the urging of his fellow, and speech is not an act (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:1).

and he does not transgress this negative commandment until he takes the item he coveted. For although the essence of the prohibition of coveting is the urging, one does not transgress the prohibition if the coveting did not reach the stage of an act of actually acquiring the item.

once he thought in his heart how he might buy this thing from him and his heart was enticed by it, he transgressed a negative commandment. This speaks of one who thought how to obtain his desire, but mere desire alone is not included in the prohibition (see Eight Chapters of Maimonides, chapter 6).
and desire is only in the heart alone. Desire in itself is a mental act and not a practical one.
even though he offered them much money. That he offered them a high payment.

from the deed of Ahab and Naboth. Ahab, king of Israel, coveted the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, and when Naboth would not agree to sell it to him, Ahab and Jezebel arranged to have him killed so that Ahab would receive the vineyard (I Kings, chapter 21).
"so are the ways of everyone greedy for gain; it takes away the life of its owners". Anyone who robs his fellow takes his life, even if only the value of a perutah.
it is an enactment of the Sages that they do not accept from him. One should not take the value of the robbed item from him.
in order to bring the upright path closer for the repentant. To ease matters for one who wants to return to the upright path (see also Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 4:5).

and even if the robber died and it is in the hands of his sons, it returns to its owners in kind. And this is not considered a change of possession that acquires together with despair (below 5:3). As for the obligation of the sons of a robber who died to return when the robbed item no longer exists, see below 5:5-6.
he acquired it by the change. And he does not need to return the robbed item itself, but pays the victim its value.
and pays its value as at the time of the robbery. According to what it was worth when it was robbed.
by oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in the interpretation of the verses.
the robber acquired all the improvement that it improved after despair. As explained below 5:6.
rabbinically, for the sake of the repentant. The Sages enacted that the robber acquire the improvement after despair in order to make it easier for him to return the robbed item.
the buyer acquired it through despair and change of possession. And the same law applies to a thief (see Hilchot Genevah 5:3).

one who robs and improves and sells or bequeaths before despair, etc.. The robber himself acquires only the improvement after despair, but if he sold or bequeathed the robbed item, the buyer or heir acquires the improvement even without despair, and this is an enactment of the Sages (see Bava Kamma 96a).

and the victim returns and takes the value of the improvement from the robber, for he had not despaired. Between the robber and the victim the law remains that he does not acquire improvement made before despair, and therefore the victim collects from the robber the value of the improvement that he paid to the heir or buyer.

and likewise if the buyer or heir improved it, etc.. When the buyer or heir themselves improved the robbed item, they acquire the improvement even if the owners had not despaired, and the victim collects the improvement from the robber.
even if the gentile improved it, it returns to its owners. And he does not pay the gentile for improvement, for the gentile is not included in this enactment (Bava Kamma 96a).

the gentile sold it to a Jew after improving it... and if the victim seized it, we do not take it from his hand. This case was not decided in the Gemara (there), and because of the doubt we do not take money from one who holds it. But if the victim seized the improvement we do not take it from him, since he is now the one in possession.
we have already explained. Above halachot 1-2, and compare Hilchot Genevah 1:11-12.
and it grew. It grew wool.
he pays as at the time of the robbery. He returns the robbed item and the victim pays him for the improvement.
he pays the value of a cow about to give birth and the value of a ewe about to be sheared. And he acquired the offspring and the fleece because they came after despair.

it is still in its owners' possession even though the robber is liable for its accidents. Although the robber is liable for every accident and bears full responsibility like an owner, he does not have the law of an owner.
and consecrated. The animal as an offering.

and slaughtered after the owners despaired. After the consecration the owners despaired and then he slaughtered the animal outside the Temple (Mirkevet HaMishneh, which resolves the Raavad's objection in his critical notes).

it is in the robber's possession only from the moment he consecrated it, etc.. In Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot (18:14) it is explained that if he stole or robbed an animal and consecrated it and after despair slaughtered it outside, he is liable to karet like one who slaughters sacred offerings outside. And although it is not possible to consecrate something that is not one's own before despair, it is explained there that the Sages placed it in his possession in order to be strict with him so that he is liable to karet for slaughtering sacred offerings outside. And here it is explained that placing the animal in the robber's possession is from the time of the consecration onward and not already from the time of the robbery, so that he not gain the improvement from then (Mirkevet HaMishneh and Yad Peshutah).

if it was lean and he fattened it, even before despair he takes from the victim the improvement of the fattening. Some explained that this law too is for the sake of the repentant, that for improvement on which he spent money they enacted that he acquire it even before despair (Or Sameach and others; and see Even HaEzel, Nizkei Mamon 7:12, who explained differently; and compare Hilchot Genevah 1:11).
to its original state. To its initial state before it changed.
they return to being boards. They return to being wooden boards.
he must grind. Crumble.
a tongue. A raw piece.
he must return it to being a tongue. He must return it to being a tongue.
and planed them. Smoothed and polished them.
or dug in them. Carved in them to make them into containers or to carve another part of the vessel.
he beat it. Struck its fibers to separate them.
and whitened it. Cleaned it.
spun. Spun threads ready for weaving a garment.
and made it dust. Crumbled it.
and polished them and renewed them. Smoothed their surface and cleaned them.
they become dull. They become covered with a dark layer.
he robbed an attached palm tree and cut it down, he did not acquire it. Since its name was and remained a palm tree (Bava Kamma 96a).

he cut it into sections and made it into beams, he acquired. For this is a complete change, but if he merely cut it down and chopped it into sections and did not make beams of them, he did not acquire, because these are sections of a palm tree and not something else entirely (there).
if he cut them into boards until their name changed, he acquired. If he cut the beam into planks, this is a complete change.
he robbed leaves and made them into broom. He split the palm leaves into two parts in each leaf and made it into a sort of broom (Rashi, Bava Kamma 96a).
he robbed a lamb and it became a ram. He robbed a small lamb and kept it until it grew up and became a ram.
this is a change in his possession and he acquired it. Although he did not do an act with his hands, a substantive change occurred in the robbed item and he acquired it.
he robbed a vessel and broke it, we do not assess for him the depreciation. He cannot return the broken vessel and pay only the loss in value of the vessel according to the assessors' estimate.

for this is an enactment for the owners. And therefore although the vessel was broken or depreciated and a change was made in it, the robber did not acquire the item (and see the Gra, section 354 subsection 13, and Ketzot HaChoshen there subsection 3, who found difficulty in this; and compare Hilchot Genevah 1:15).
and became more expensive. It rose in price.

but the improvement of the price rise, if the robbed item exists, returns in kind. As for acquiring the improvement of the price rise when the robbed item no longer exists, see the beginning of the next chapter.
and it became more expensive with him and stood at four. It rose in price without any change occurring in it and its price stood at four dinars.

if he broke the jar, etc.. In principle the robber pays for the robbed item according to its value at the time of the robbery (Mishnah Bava Kamma 9:1), but when he destroyed it with his hands he pays according to its value at that time (see Bava Metzia 43a).
a wrapper. A covering, like a bag or box, made of palm leaves and the like, in which fresh dates are sold (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 16:5).
and when he sells them one by one he sells for ten. If he sells the dates separately he will receive ten coins for them.
and the victim cannot say to him, I would have sold them one by one. And therefore the value of the robbed item is ten.
and the same law applies to one who damages. Also in a case where he damaged his fellow's property we assess the damage in the same way.

and likewise anything similar to this with ordinary property, but with consecrated property it is not so, rather he pays ten. For an ordinary person the Sages were lenient to assess by the overall value, since we find that the Torah was lenient in a similar matter in monetary damages (see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 4:13 and the explanation there), but with consecrated property they were not lenient (see Bava Metzia 99b).
it grew lean. It became thin, weakened.
for example, illnesses that have no cure. That have no remedies that would help them.
or the king invalidated it. Who decreed that the coin could not be used for payment.
this is like one who robbed a vessel and broke it, etc.. And the robber takes the robbed item and pays the victim its full value (see above 2:15).
and it is accepted in another country. It can be used for payment in another place.
or terumah and it became impure. And it is forbidden to eat.
chametz and Pesach passed over it. And it became forbidden for eating and benefit.
an animal on which a transgression was committed. For example, it was mated with by a person and was disqualified from being offered.
or that was disqualified from being offered. For example, a blemish developed in it.
or that was going out to be stoned. And it is forbidden for benefit, such as an ox that killed a person.
he must return its value as at the time of the robbery. And not according to its value when it was lost, as explained above 5:2.

therefore, etc.. Since he must pay if it is lost, it turns out it still has value even though it is forbidden for benefit, and therefore if he denied the robbery and swore about it, he must pay its value plus a fifth and a guilt offering (as below 7:1).
even though he transgressed a negative commandment. Of robbery (above 1:3).

we penalize him, even outside the Land. Although ordinarily judges outside the Land do not judge fines and do not even collect fines enacted by the Sages (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:8-9), in exceptional cases it is permitted to act by emergency measure outside the ordinary law and to penalize one who breaks through the fences of religion or behaves violently (see there 24:6).
and we assess the wages or the improvement that he improved in the animal. We estimate how much the robber gained or how much his property improved because of the work.
the one who seizes. Holds by force.
he is exempt, for a person is pleased that his slave not be idle. Even though the slave becomes thin from the work, the slave's owner prefers this to an idle slave (Bava Kamma 97a).
if it is not made for hire. If the owner is not accustomed to rent it out.

if he went down to it in the manner of renting, etc.. That he intended to pay rent. In this case he can be judged as a renter who must pay rent, or as a robber (like one who borrows without knowledge, below halachah 15) who pays the depreciation, and therefore the owner of the ship will choose what to collect from him.
even though this resident is accustomed to rent a place for himself. That the resident is accustomed to rent a place for himself to live in.
for this one benefits and this one does not lose. The owners do not lose because of the resident's benefit, and therefore he does not have to pay them.
even though this one is not accustomed to rent. And it turns out that the resident does not gain by not paying rent for the courtyard.
and soaked dyes. Dyeing materials soaked in water separately from the wool.

he pays him the value of what he lost in the wool, etc.. When they assess the value of the dyed wool that the robber returns to the victim, the robber is at a disadvantage: if the value of the dyed wool decreased because of the dyeing he pays the difference, since he damaged the wool; and if the wool improved because of the dyes on it, he does not pay for what it improved (see Mirkevet HaMishneh).

and if the injured party seized the value of what was lacking from the dyes, we do not take it from his hand. For besides returning the wool, the robber must return the dyes. But there is a doubt about this whether returning the dyed wool is also considered returning the dye he took, or not. Therefore the court does not obligate him to pay for the dye, but if the owner seized the value of the dye from the dyer's property, we do not take it from his hand.
one who lays a hand on a deposit. He took the deposit that was deposited with him in order to bring it into his possession as a robber.

by means of his son, his slave and his agent, he is a robber and is liable for its accidents. Although ordinarily there is no agent for a transgression, with laying a hand the Sages learned that the agent's act binds the one who sent him (Kiddushin 42b).
he is not liable for its responsibility. As a robber; rather his law is still that of a guardian.
but he took the deposit... in order to lay a hand on it. That he brought it into his possession as a robber.
he became liable for its accidents. Of the jar and all the wine in it, since he lifted the whole jar.
the purse. A wallet.
and anything like a purse of things that are not one body. A container with several separate things in it that he lifted and intends to take only one thing from it.
this is a doubt. Perhaps only with a jar is he liable for all the wine because all the wine is one unit, and not in lifting a purse in which each dinar stands by itself.
it is in its owners' possession. And its law remains that of a deposit.
for he did not lift the jar. And the jar did not pass into his responsibility.

and if it turned sour he pays the value of all of it. If the wine remaining in the jar turned sour he is liable, since removing the revi'it of wine can cause the rest to turn sour (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Metzia 3:12).
and one of them took it and used it. One person took the item from them and used it.
until he returns it to the owners. And it is not enough that he return it to the one he took it from.

one who seizes a pledge from the hand of the borrower without the court's authorization. But a court agent is permitted to take the pledge by force from the borrower, provided he does not enter his house (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 3:4).

the Sages imposed a fine on robbers, etc.. And the reason for the fine is "so that damages and lawlessness among people do not multiply" (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevuot 7:3, and compare Hilchot Chovel u-Mazik 5:4).
one who entered his fellow's house to take a pledge. And it is known that he entered for this purpose, and since it is forbidden to take a pledge by force he is treated as a robber (above 3:16).
under his wings. Under the wings of his garment.

the homeowner swears while holding an object. While holding a Torah scroll (Hilchot Shevuot 11:8, and see there halachah 11), according to the law of those who swear and take (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:2).
where he claimed things that he is presumed to have. That it is plausible that the claimant had such things in his possession.
for it is presumed that such things as he claimed are deposited with him. That it is plausible that such things are given to him for safekeeping.

even if he said, "I never entered," since he contradicts the witnesses, he is exempt. Although it was shown by the witnesses that he lied about his entering the house, he is not established as a liar regarding his claim that he did not take vessels from the house.
he swears the heset oath. A light oath (without holding an object) that the Sages imposed on a defendant in cases where he is exempt from a severe oath (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:3).

for it is possible that he entered to rob and did not rob. And therefore the fact that he entered to take a pledge does not testify that he actually took vessels from his house, and they did not enact that the claimant swear and take.
there was one witness testifying that he entered. For example, he testifies that he entered to take a pledge (Maggid Mishneh), which is forbidden as robbery (see above 3:16).
since the witness does not know what was under his wings. For if he had known, he would have obligated him to take the Torah oath (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:1).

for he is not established as a robber except by two witnesses. Since the Sages' enactment that he swears and takes when it is not known how much he took is based on his having been established as a robber, if there is only one witness that he took, he was not established as a robber, and the claimant does not swear and take.
just as the homeowner swears and takes. When there are witnesses that he robbed and it is not known what he took.

so too the homeowner's guardian. Who guards for the homeowner. And his law is not that of a witness but of the homeowner himself, and after he swears how much he took, the homeowner collects from the robber.

even the guardian's wife. For the deposit was given to the guardian with the understanding that his wife and household could also serve as guardians (see Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 4:8-9), and therefore she too can swear.
he was there. In the victim's house at the time of the robbery.
his hired worker. A temporary worker.

they do not swear and take. For it is doubtful whether they too are considered entrusted with guarding the house, and therefore it is doubtful whether their oath is effective, and money cannot be taken on their word.

and we do not make the robber swear because he is suspect regarding oaths. Since he is established as a robber, he is suspected of swearing a false oath and we do not make him swear (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 2:2).

the homeowner pronounces a general ban. By enactment of the Geonim, in certain cases where a person suspects another of claiming falsely against him and cannot obligate him to an oath, he can impose a ban (curse) in general on anyone who lies against him in that matter without mentioning the suspect's name (see Hilchot Sheluchin ve-Shutafin 3:11, Maggid Mishneh, Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:4).

and even if the robber admitted that he robbed part, he returns only the part he admitted. And he is not liable for the oath of one who admits part, since he is liable for it only in a definite claim.
this too is a fine, etc.. Compare Hilchot Mechirah 20:3.
he swears the heset oath like any defendant. See above 5:4 for explanation.
the Torah oath... like anyone who admits part. The oath by the Torah that a defendant is obligated to take when he admitted part of the sum the claimant claimed (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:1).
for he was not established as a robber by witnesses. And therefore he is not suspect regarding the oath.
even though he admitted that he took a pledge without authorization. And transgressed the prohibition of robbery (above 3:16).

since there are no witnesses there... he swears and collects his debt from the pledge. For if there are witnesses that he took it he must return the pledge even if it is known that the borrower owes him (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 3:4).

for the mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted. Just as the reason to obligate him is based on his statement that he took the vessels, so one can rely on his claim that he took them for his debt in order to exempt him.
as will be explained in Hilchot To'en. 1:2.
and even though this homeowner was accustomed to sell his vessels. And taking out the vessels in itself does not arouse suspicion.

for anyone who enters his fellow's house not in his presence and takes vessels from there... is presumed a robber. And therefore he is not believed even though the manner of taking the vessels is not suspicious (and compare Hilchot Genevah 5:12, where in the opposite situation, when a person took in the presence of the homeowner, he is believed, unless there is a combination of several suspicious circumstances).
and there is no oath here. The homeowner does not need to swear what was taken from him.
and after he returns it he returns and claims, etc.. If he still insists that he took them lawfully, he can sue the homeowner in a separate case.
for had there been witnesses there, he would have been liable to pay. Since he also testifies to what he took, for the vessels were visible.
liable to an oath. To deny the witness, and he is obligated to swear by Torah law.

and he cannot swear, for he does not deny the witness. One who is obligated to take an oath against one witness, but who admits the witness's testimony and makes a different claim to exempt himself, cannot exempt himself even by swearing to his present claim (see Hilchot To'en VeNitan 4:8).
and anyone who is obligated to swear and cannot swear must pay. One who was sued and became obligated to a Torah oath but cannot swear must pay (for further examples see Hilchot To'en VeNitan 4:7-8).
there was an incident with a certain man, etc.. See Babylonian Talmud, Shevuot 32b.
and he cannot swear, for he admitted as the witness said. And consequently he must pay, as explained in the previous halakhah.

and had there been no witness at all, he would have sworn a heset oath that he seized what was his. As is the law of a defendant who is not obligated to a severe oath (see above halakhah 4 in the commentary).

and by this law one judges every similar case anywhere. That when a person is obligated to a Torah oath and cannot swear, he pays (see Hilchot She'elah UFikadon 5:6, Hilchot To'en VeNitan 4:7-8, and others).

and had there been two, he would have been liable to pay. If there had been two witnesses to the seizure, he would have been liable to pay, since it is known that he seized and how much he seized from the one who seized. Therefore, when there is one witness, we judge by the rule that any testimony that obligates monetary payment through two witnesses obligates a Torah oath through one witness. It turns out that he is liable to a Torah oath, but since he cannot swear because he does not deny the witness's words, he must pay.
as we explained. Above halakhah 13.

he pays the twenty that he admitted he seized. As explained in the previous halakhah, but since, unlike the previous halakhah, the victim claims that he seized a hundred, he must swear to his claim in order to be exempt from the eighty.
and he swears a Torah oath on the rest. As in the law of one who admits part of a claim, and this is the view of the Geonim (see Shakh, Choshen Mishpat 75, subsection 19).
for he admitted nothing. Rather he claimed that he took what was his.
the householder says, I had twenty vessels in my house. But he does not know how many the robber took.

he must return the ten, because he is obligated to swear and cannot swear. Regarding those ten that he says he took lawfully, he is obligated to swear against the witness but cannot swear, because he admits the witness's words.

and he does not swear on the rest... because he cannot make a definite claim against the robber. For he does not know with certainty that this is the one who took them, and one does not swear a heset oath on a claim of "perhaps" (Hilchot To'en VeNitan 1:7).
to help him with his alteration so that he acquires it. To assist him in making an alteration in the stolen item through which he acquires it.
strengthens the hands of transgressors. For by buying from him he encourages him to steal more (compare Hilchot Genevah 5:1).

and violates "and before the blind do not place a stumbling block". For from this verse we learn the prohibition of causing a person to stumble or strengthening him in committing a transgression (see Hilchot Rotzeach 12:14).
even after despair. Since even after despair the stolen item belongs to its owner (Maggid Mishneh).
or to enter it in the heat, etc.. To shelter in it from the sun or the rain.
like the law of one who lives in his fellow's courtyard without his knowledge. Above 3:9.

one who stole palm trees and made a bridge of them, it is forbidden to cross it. Since no alteration was made in them, they were not acquired by the robber (above 2:10, and see ibid. halakhah 13 for the case of stealing attached palm trees).
one who transgressed and ate the stolen item. Another person who is not the robber.

after despair is exempt from paying. Although it is forbidden to benefit from stolen property even after despair (above halakhah 2), if he transgressed and ate from it after despair he is exempt from paying (for the reason for the exemption see Tosafot, Bava Kamma 111b, s.v. gazal), and the victim collects the value of the stolen item from the robber.

and if he ate before despair and the owners wish to collect from the one who ate, they collect, etc.. The victim collects from the one who ate or from the robber, since both are liable to pay: the robber because he stole, and the one who ate because he damaged his property.

one who stole and died... if he left land, they are liable to pay, etc.. In all these cases the obligation to pay is on the robber and not on his sons. When he dies and leaves land, his debt is collected from the land inherited by the orphans, since it is pledged to their father's debt, but movable property is not pledged to a debt and is not collected from (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 11:7).
the Geonim already enacted, etc.. See also Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 11:11.
whether they ate or did not eat, etc.. Regardless of whether they became liable to pay on their own because of the eating, or only because of their father who stole.
the law of one who buys movable property, etc.. But for land they did not make the market enactment (see below 9:9 and Shulchan Aruch 371:1).
like one who buys from a thief. See Hilchot Genevah 5:2-3.

if he is a known robber, they did not apply to him the market enactment. Therefore if he bought them before despair, he returns them without compensation, and the buyer collects his money from the robber (ibid.).
and he again claims from the robber the value of the stolen item. The victim claims from the robber the money he paid to the buyer.

and if the owners had already despaired, the buyer acquired the stolen item itself. He acquired the stolen item itself since there was despair and a change of possession (above 2:3), and the victim collects the value of his loss from the robber.
from the robber. From his property, even if it is not known that he benefited from a stolen item.
and if it was a small amount of his. A minority of his property belongs to him and did not reach him by theft.
for this thing. That he wants to benefit from.
until it is known for certain that this item is stolen in his hand. As above, halakhah 2.
the tax collectors. Collectors of duties.
and the bandits. Armed robbers.
because their occupation is robbery. See below halakhah 11.
and we do not exchange dinars from their box. One does not change money from coins found in the box used for collecting the toll.
his garment. His clothing.

because this is like a sale, and the presumption is that the owners despaired of them. Since he received it in exchange for his garment, it is like a sale, and since the presumption is also that the owners despaired of it, he acquired it by despair and change of possession.

and he does not know for certain that this is stolen. The commentators discussed what need there is for this reason, since there is despair and change of possession, which suffice to acquire stolen property. Some explained that if it were certainly stolen, his law would be that of one who bought from a known thief after despair (see Hilchot Genevah 5:3), and he would have to pay the value of the garment (Sma, Choshen Mishpat 369, subsection 9; and see a different explanation in Kesef Mishneh).
a pious person. One who is scrupulous in his conduct (see below 14:13).
when the tax collector is a gentile. Whose presumption is that he collects more than the fixed toll and takes the difference for himself (Maggid Mishneh).
a tax collector who appoints himself. Without authorization from the king.
a tax collector appointed by the king who has no fixed rate. He does not collect a set, fixed sum.
and it is known that this person is trustworthy and adds nothing to what the king decreed. For an ordinary tax collector is presumed to take more than he should by law (Hilchot Edut 10:4).
because the law of the king is law, etc.. And it is not theft; on the contrary, one must act according to it, and one who evades the tax violates the prohibition of theft.
the king's portion. The king's share.
whether the king was a gentile or a king of Israel. For even theft from a gentile is forbidden, as above 1:2.
on every single person. Such as a poll tax.
or decreed that anyone who violates this matter. That he not pay that tax.
or anyone found in the field at the time of the threshing floor. One in whose possession the crop is at the time the crop is gathered.
and the buyer. The purchaser.
and the owners cannot remove it from his hand. The owner of the field cannot claim the field in court.
their lien. The monetary right they have in the field.
for they sell the fields for the tax fixed on the fields. That if he did not pay the tax on the field, it can be sold.
he collects only from the person himself. And not from his land.
and if they sold the field for the tax on the head. If they acted unlawfully and sold his field because he did not pay a tax imposed on his person individually.
a king whose laws, etc.. If the law is that when a person does not pay the tax on a field, another person may pay the tax and eat its produce in the meantime.
for the law of the king is law, as we said. Above halakhah 11.
and likewise a king who decreed, etc.. That a person who does not pay tax will be enslaved to the one who paid the tax; and see also Hilchot Avadim 1:8.
he may work him more than enough. Even more than the tax money he paid for him, and there is no interest here (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 5:17).
but he may not work him as a slave. For it is forbidden to enslave him like a Canaanite slave by degrading or hard labor and the like, as explained in Hilchot Avadim 1:6-7.
it is permitted to cross it... it is permitted to benefit from it. And they are not forbidden for benefit like the stolen item mentioned above in halakhah 3.
a king whose coin circulates in those lands. Whose rule is accepted by the people of the land (for issuing coinage in the name of a ruler is a declaration of his independence and rule).

beams, stones, wood, and the like that the river swept away, etc.. The commentators explained that this refers specifically to a case where the owners could save the beams and stones, even with difficulty. But if they cannot save them in any way, there is no need to know that they despaired (see Maggid Mishneh and others, and see below 11:10).
if the owners despaired of them. It is known that they gave up the possibility of getting them back.
and needless to say if the owners were pursuing them. For it is clear from their behavior that they did not give up their property.
one who rescues from the river. Draws out of the river.
and from the depths of the sea. The sea bottom.
and from the current of a river. The flow of the river.
the troop. A group of soldiers.
the fire. A conflagration.
the hyena. It seems that here a hyena is meant (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 1:4; Aruch HaShalem, entries "bardelas" and "afa").
if he knows for certain that the owners despaired, they are his. Because it is permitted to take for oneself a lost item of which its owners have despaired (below 14:1-4).
a bandit. An armed robber.
they are his, because it is assumed that the owners despaired. And there is despair, and also a change of possession when they came into his hands.

for the owners know that gentiles take back from the robber's hand, etc.. The judges of the gentiles do not require valid witnesses who saw the act of robbery, and therefore the owners rely on being able to recover the stolen item for themselves through their courts.
shachalayim. A plant eaten for food and medicine.
because they ruin the flax for the owner of the field. They harm the flax crop, and therefore the owner is not particular about one who takes them.
for they have already ruined what they ruined. And now the owners want them.
and if they were on the boundary. At the edge of the plot.
they are forbidden even when they are moist. Because the owner of the field does not want them uprooted from there.
we already explained in Nizkei Mamon. Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 13:14.
his straw and his stalks. The remains of grain and legumes after the kernels have been removed, which he takes out to the public domain so that passersby trample on them and they become fertilizer.
they are not subject to theft. Because he took them out without permission, the Sages penalized him.
the dung. Animal excrement.
at the time of removal of fertilizers. Times when the Sages permitted taking fertilizer and dung out to the public domain (ibid. halakhah 15).

and if not at the time of removal of fertilizers, they are liable on account of theft. For even though he took them out in violation, the Sages did not penalize him, since they do not improve by being taken out (see ibid.).
his vessels. His clothing.
until the other comes. The owner of the clothing that is now with him.
in the craftsman's house. One who repairs clothing.
if the craftsman's wife and sons gave it to him. Who are not expert in the garments in the craftsman's possession, and we cannot rely on their having done so knowingly.
or the craftsman gave it to him and said to him, take your vessels. And apparently he mistakenly thought these were his clothes.
he may use it, etc.. One may rely on the possibilities according to which the vessel was given to him permissibly.
or the owner of the vessel instructed the craftsman to sell it. And the giving was permitted (see Ramah, Bava Batra 46a).
the Sages forbade on account of theft. And by Torah law they carry no prohibition of theft.
within the settlement. In an inhabited place.

for he is taking the property of others unlawfully. Although it is not entirely the property of others, since they come to the dovecote on their own and the owner of the dovecote has not acquired them, the Sages nevertheless said they are like his property.
and bring. Draw after him.

anyone who does this with other birds or wild animals and livestock. Animals over which there is no complete ownership because they did not fully come into the victim's possession, such as dovecote pigeons (see Sma, Choshen Mishpat 270, subsection 2).
traps. Hunting snares.
unless he distances himself from the settlement. Since the pigeons of the settlement also fly outside the settlement.
four mil. About 4 km.
and if it was a settlement of vineyards, etc.. If the area is planted with vineyards, one may not hunt near it even if the vineyard area is a hundred mil, although it is not inhabited by people.
and likewise he may not spread a net among dovecotes. In an area where dovecotes stand.
even though they are his, etc.. And there is no prohibition on account of that dovecote.

of a gentile. And theft that is permitted by Torah law and forbidden by rabbinic law, such as this, was not forbidden regarding a gentile (see below halakhah 11, and see Shitah Mekubetzet, Bava Kamma 83a in the name of the Rid).
and even if he distanced himself a hundred mil from the settlement. For pigeons fly from dovecote to dovecote and reach a great distance.
and likewise the Sages forbade hunting pigeons. Although he does not draw them to himself.
so that the young pigeons not be drawn. The young birds in his dovecote, which wander off up to fifty cubits from the dovecote (below 15:18).

and if he bought it from another... it is in its presumption. If he bought from another person a dovecote that already stood near another's field, it is not forbidden, because it was established as a damage and in neighbor damages, presumption of right is effective (see Hilchot Shecheinim 11:4-6).
a beit rova. An area in which a quarter-kav of seed is sown (slightly more than ten square cubits).
with pebbles. Small stones.
although he took it with the owners' consent. And therefore it is not theft by Torah law.
and jest. From the word for mockery.
since he took his fellow's property for free as a joke and jest, it is theft. Since this is not a complete gift, he did not acquire it, and he has in his hand money that is not his.

and one who plays dice with a gentile has no prohibition of theft. Because theft that is permitted by Torah law was not forbidden regarding a gentile, and furthermore here it was done with the gentile's consent (Sma).
but he has the prohibition of one who engages in idle matters. See Hilchot Edut 10:4.
snares. Hunting traps.

theft by rabbinic law, because they have not yet reached the hand of the one who acquires them. This prohibition is rabbinic because snares do not acquire the game for the owner of the snare. But if the snare was made as a vessel, it belongs to the owner of the snare and one who takes from it is a robber (Hilchot Zechiyah 1:3).
and a river that flows. That runs.
they belong to everyone. And everyone is permitted to drink from them, not only the people of the place through which they flow (compare Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 5:3 and see the explanation there).
one who beats the top of the olive tree. Strikes the olive tree to make the olives fall.
forgotten olives. Olives the owners forgot to pick, which are part of the gifts to the poor (Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 1:6).
and took them from the ground. After they fell.
acquisition by rabbinic law. Like pigeons, above halakhah 7.
a swarm of bees. A group of bees.
or prevented it from its owners if it came into his domain. Prevented the owners from retrieving them if they came into his domain.
and if he caused damage. In the course of returning it.

but he may not cut the branch in order to pay money. He may not cut a branch on which the bees gathered even if he intends to pay for the damage, since this is a loss that cannot be undone (Meiri, Bava Kamma 114a).
from here this swarm came out. And the person from whose domain they left can bring them back to himself.
provided that they speak innocently. Without intending to testify, since they are not fit for testimony (Hilchot Edut 9:1).
and the owners are pursuing the swarm and asking where it settled. And they are not making a mere claim.
even though a woman or a minor is not fit for testimony. Even when they speak innocently (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 114b).

since acquisition of bees is by rabbinic law, they believed them in it. Even if the swarm was originally in the domain of the one in whose hands it now is, he has no ownership by Torah law, and therefore their testimony suffices to take it from him.
he cannot be made to give it up through the judges. He cannot be sued in court for it (see also below 17:12).
he does not add a fifth. To the payment of the principal.
he does not add a fifth, etc.. See below 7:1-2.
anyone who became liable for money to his fellow Yisrael. As detailed in the next halakhah.
and denied it and swore falsely. Answered that he does not owe him as he claimed, and also swore to this.
he must return to him the principal he denied, etc.. And he violates the negative commandment "and you shall not deal falsely, each man with his fellow" (Leviticus 19:11, Hilchot Shevuot 1:8-9).
one who defrauds. One who denies a payment he owes (see above 1:4).
and denied it. Denied the owner's claim.
and some money remained with him. After the partnership was dissolved and divided.

anything for which, had he admitted, he would have been liable to pay by law, and he denied and swore, etc.. For the details of denial of money that obligates on account of an oath concerning a deposit, see Hilchot Shevuot chapters 7-8.

for it is said, "and deals falsely with his fellow regarding a deposit," etc.. And later in the verse it says: "or anything about which he swore falsely, he shall repay it in full and add a fifth to it." From here it follows that for every denial of money one pays the principal and the fifth.
for example, his father stole or robbed, etc.. And died, and his son inherited him.

and the son knows, etc.. That his father is liable, and denied this and swore falsely. For if he did not know that his father was liable and swore unintentionally, he is exempt from the fifth, since one is not liable for a fifth for an unintentional oath (Hilchot Shevuot 1:10-11).
but if his father stole and died, etc.. In which case the stolen item is like a deposit with him, and when he denies the victim's claim he becomes liable on his own account.

the heir pays the principal and the fifth. Although the payment of the fifth is meant for atonement (below halakhah 8), since the father became obligated in it, it has the law of a monetary debt that falls on the inherited property (see above 5:5).
he pays the principal only. For the fifth is owed only if the one who swore admitted.

and either way the heir is exempt from the guilt offering. Whether the one who swore admitted or his son admitted, for the guilt offering is an obligation on the father, who committed the transgression.

and likewise one who stole less than the value of a perutah and denied and swore is not liable for the fifth. And he is also exempt from an offering, but he violated the negative commandment of a vain oath because he swore falsely (Hilchot Shevuot 7:16).
for less than the value of a perutah is not money. For purposes of payments, as above 1:6.
how much is the fifth? One quarter of the principal. That it is not a fifth of the value of the stolen item (the principal), but a fifth of the total payment (principal and fifth).
and he stands by his denial. But if he admitted after witnesses came, he is liable for the fifth and the guilt offering.
except for the value of a perutah. But for less than the value of a perutah there is no obligation of return (above 1:6).
and not to his agent. A person who is accustomed to run errands for the victim, but did not appoint him to receive this stolen item.

and if he brought the stolen item and the fifth to the court, etc.. The Sages enacted that he may bring the stolen item and the fifth to the court, since there are cases where the costs of returning exceed the value of the stolen item (Bava Kamma 103b).
becomes expensive. Becomes more costly.
as we explained. Above halakhah 10.
one who returns the principal to the owners. And remains liable for the fifth.
the fifth becomes like the principal for all purposes. For once he became liable for it as atonement, its law is like any monetary debt.

until the fifth diminishes so that he denies and swears over less than the value of a perutah. Each time the fifth shrinks to a fifth of the previous fifth (that is, a quarter of it, above halakhah 7), and when it is less than the value of a perutah and he swore over it, he is exempt from a fifth, since he is not liable for a fifth when he swears over less than the value of a perutah (above halakhah 7).
one who had a deposit with him, etc.. See also Hilchot Shevuot 9:15.
or it changed. In which case he acquired it for himself and pays its value.
he gives the principal and the fifth to the heirs. If he admitted that he stole.

and if the stolen item still exists, he must remove the stolen item itself from his possession. The Sages taught that the robber has no remedy until he removes the stolen item itself from his possession or the victim forgives him (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 9:10), and his right as an heir in the stolen item he cannot exercise in the item itself but only in its equivalent.

he gives the stolen item and the fifth to his brothers and settles accounts with them. He gives his brothers the stolen item and the fifth, and his share of the inheritance, including the proportional share he has in the stolen item and the fifth, he takes from the rest of the property they inherited (Maggid Mishneh and Kesef Mishneh). For example, if there are five brothers, and the stolen item and fifth are worth five zuzim and the rest of the inheritance is twenty zuz, he gives his brothers the stolen item and the fifth, and the inheritance together is twenty-five zuz, of which he has five zuz, four from the twenty and one from the five he paid, and he takes all five from the other property and not from the stolen item.
to his sons. Of the robber.
to his creditor or in his loan. As repayment to one to whom he owes (such as a wife's ketubah), or to one who lent to him (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 9:10).

since the stolen item itself left his possession, he is released, etc.. For there is no obstacle to his deriving benefit from the stolen item, only that the stolen item itself not be in his possession.

provided that he informs them and says, this is my father's stolen property. For if he does not say so, it appears that he is giving them from his own and is not considered to have removed the stolen item from his possession (see Commentary on the Mishnah there).
and he recorded everything to him as a loan. He defined the payment of the stolen item and the fifth as a debt and forgave him the return of the stolen item itself.

and afterward the convert died. A convert has no heirs except his sons born after he converted, and if he has no sons, upon his death his property becomes ownerless and whoever holds it acquires it (Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 1:6).

even though he acquired the stolen item. Already from the moment he recorded it as a loan, and apparently it is as if he returned the stolen item to him and only a monetary debt remains on him, nevertheless he must remove the stolen item from his possession.
where he admitted to two. And became obligated for the principal and the fifth to the convert, and when he died he acquired them for himself.
he must pay the principal and the fifth. If he admitted after the convert's death (Merkevet HaMishneh).
to the kohanim. When he brings the guilt offering to the Temple, he pays the kohanim the principal and the fifth before offering it (below halakhah 13).
a watch. The group of kohanim serving that week (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:3).
from oral tradition they learned, etc.. The Sages received by tradition that this verse was said regarding one who swore to a convert and the convert died before the robber admitted to him.

and this guilt offering mentioned here. The text of the verse: "And if the man has no kinsman to whom restitution may be made, the restitution that is made shall go to the Lord, to the kohen, in addition to the ram of atonement with which atonement is made for him." The guilt offering mentioned in the verse here is the stolen item or its value that the robber must bring in addition to the ram of atonement, which is the guilt offering sacrifice.
for Scripture called it a guilt offering. From here the Sages learned that the law of a stolen item that is returned is like that of an offering.
and we do not offer at night. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 4:1.

and the kohanim do not divide the convert's theft against the convert's theft, etc.. The portions of offerings due to the kohanim are divided among the kohanim of the watch serving that week, and they may not exchange a share in one offering for a share in another offering (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:15-16). In the same way they may not exchange payment of one theft for payment of another theft.
a convert's theft that does not contain the value of a perutah for each kohen... the one who returns it has not fulfilled the obligation of return. See Piskei VeShitot.
and why is "man" stated regarding a convert's theft. "And if the man has no kinsman."
for with a man you must investigate and search for him whether he has heirs. When the convert is a "man," that is, an adult.
rather his presumption is that he has no heirs. Because a minor cannot father children (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 69a).

the kohanim, regarding a convert's theft, are like recipients of gifts, etc.. The giving to the kohanim is not defined as payment of theft to the owners but as priestly gifts (like the firstborn and terumah), and the amount of the gift is determined as of the time of the theft (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 110b).
for it is forbidden for benefit. Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 1:4.
as we explained. Above 3:4.

this one did not acquire the stolen item that is under his hand. And he cannot say that since the stolen item must in any case reach the kohanim and it is under his hand, he can acquire it (compare Hilchot Arachin 4:23).
the watch. The watch of kohanim serving that week.

the sons of the robber inherit the money of the stolen item or the stolen item itself. For the obligation of bringing the stolen item to the kohanim rests on the father during his lifetime as atonement, and his sons do not need atonement (Meiri, Bava Kamma 110a).

and the guilt offering is left to graze until it develops a blemish. Because one does not offer a guilt offering whose owner died. Its law is to be sold after it develops a blemish and the money is given to the fund from which communal voluntary burnt offerings are brought.
as we explained in its place. Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:14.
before atonement. Before the offering is sacrificed.
it shall be his. The kohen's.

even if the robber was a minor, whose gift is not a gift. For by Torah law a minor cannot transfer ownership (see Hilchot Mechirah 29:1 and ibid. halakhah 6). And although a minor is not included in the law of oaths and is not liable for a fifth and a guilt offering, one may say that this speaks of a minor whose father stole and swore and admitted and died, and he gave the money of the stolen item to the men of the watch. Although he did not steal, he is called a robber because his father's theft is with him (Responsa Radbaz 6, no. 2284).
to one of the watches. A watch that is not serving that week and is not entitled to priestly gifts.
its week. Its week.
he returns the money to the guilt offering. He adds the money to the guilt offering.
the established watch. The watch for which this week is its time.
we do not offer, etc.. And if he offered the sacrifice before returning the principal, he must bring another offering for his atonement (see also Hilchot Shegagot 9:7).
slaves, documents, and land have no addition of a fifth. And also no offering, because they are not included in the law of the oath concerning a deposit stated in the verse (Hilchot Shevuot 7:3-4).

and deals falsely with his fellow regarding a deposit, etc.. A deposit applies only to movable property and not to land, and the Sages learned that anything that is not complete money is not included in this law (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 117b).
and slaves are excluded, for they were likened to land. The Torah equated their law with that of land (see Hilchot Genevah 2:2).
and documents are excluded, whose body is not money. Because the value of a document is derived not from the value of the paper but from what is written in it.
and likewise if it was a convert's theft. Slaves, documents, and land.
they do not return to the kohanim. Since they are not included in the law of the oath, they are also not included in the law of a convert's theft.
and likewise land, etc.. In addition, there is a fundamental difference between land and all movable property.
and even if it was sold... and the owners despaired. Whereas ordinarily stolen property is acquired by the robber through despair and change of possession (above 2:3).
he turns to the one who sold it to him. To return to him what he paid him for it.
as will be explained. In chapter 9.
pits, trenches, and caves. Different kinds of excavations.
and ruined the springs. For example, by blocking them.
the building. Various structures built on the land, such as a house and a fence.
he must restore for him a house or field as they were at the time of the theft. To return them to their former condition.

or pay the value of what he ruined. And although he damaged the land, it is not acquired by the robber like stolen movables that changed, which are acquired by the robber (above 2:1-2); rather land always remains in its owner's possession (above 8:14).
by fire that came down from heaven. In contrast to a fire that was set, which sometimes has a responsible party who can be sued.
as we explained. Above 3:4.
oppressors by the king's power. People who seize land by force without any right.
if it is a plague of the province... he says to him, here is yours before you. As in the case where a river swept it away, where the damage was not caused by the robber.
free property. Unencumbered property, which was not sold to others after the theft.

because it is like an oral loan. Any payment a person owes by law but for which he has not yet been adjudged in court has the law of an oral loan not written in a document, and therefore it is collected only from unencumbered property (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 11:4).

and if the robber stood trial... he collects from encumbered property. Since he was adjudged by law, the debt became like a loan with a document, and if he sold some of his property afterward, the victim takes it from the buyer.
from unencumbered property. As with a field that was damaged.
and improved. Invested in the field and increased its value.
we assess. We estimate the improvement and the expense (see below 10:10).
and his hand is on the lower, etc.. He is in an inferior position, and therefore can claim only the lower amount of the two.
the expense. The cost of the investment.

and he takes the principal along with the rest of the improvement from the robber. And it turns out that overall he receives everything that was taken from him, unlike the robber, who does not receive the difference between the expense and the improvement.

the principal from encumbered property. A person who sells land is responsible to compensate the buyer for a sale that was voided, and his property is pledged to this from the time of the sale. Therefore the buyer collects the principal (the amount he paid for the land) from property that belonged to the seller (the robber) at the time of the sale, even if afterward those lands were sold to others.

and the rest of the improvement from unencumbered property. Although the robber must compensate the buyer even for what he improved, the buyer collects the improvement only from property that is in the robber's hands and not from his property that was sold, for the sake of the welfare of the world: since the amount is not fixed, people would not be able to be careful about buying land pledged for this (and see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 21:1).
he takes from the robber only the principal, etc.. In addition to the expense he takes from the victim.

or if he did not recognize it, he has from the expense only according to the amount of the improvement. Even though he bought it in good faith, because even if it had remained with him he would have had only the improvement.
we calculate against him all the produce he ate and he pays the owner of the field. Because the field is presumed to belong to its owner, and he ate produce that was not his.

and again collects them from the robber from unencumbered property. As explained in the previous halakhah regarding improvement, that it is collected only from property in the robber's hands and not from property he had that was sold to others.
and if he recognized that it was stolen, he has no produce. Because he brought it on himself.
one who sells a field that is not his. Such as a robber.
as we explained. Above 8:14.
and bought it. Acquired it lawfully.
it is established in the hand of the buyer from the robber. His purchase takes effect because the robber bought it from the victim.
therefore if the buyer claimed from the robber. That he give him what he paid for the field.
to announce the robber's property. To put it up for sale at the highest price (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 22:6).
it is not established in the hand of the buyer. And the buyer must return the field to the robber, since it now belongs to him, and he collects from him what he paid for the field.
he bequeathed it. Wrote it in a will to another person.
and likewise if it fell to the robber by inheritance. Which came to him automatically, and there is no proof that he wishes to establish it in the buyer's hand.
the robber collected it for his debt. If after the theft he collected the field because of a debt the victim owed him.
he intended to establish it in the buyer's hand. Because he chose to collect specifically the field he sold to him.
he intended to collect his debt. And this does not show that he took it so that the sale to the buyer would be completed.

for had he not troubled himself for the owners, they would not have given him a gift. And since the gift was given as payment for the effort, its law is that of a sale (for this principle see Hilchot Mechirah 29:14 and elsewhere).
and not with my knowledge. Not with my consent.
the robber has nothing. Not even compensation.
as he claimed. As he claimed.
a declaration. An advance statement that the sale he will make is not with his consent and is void.
and the law of a robber is not like the law of one who coerces his fellow. See also Hilchot Mechirah 10:5.
therefore if the coerced seller did not give a declaration, his sale stands. See ibid. halakhah 1.
a man of force. One who acts by power.
or because he has, etc.. Who claims that the Yisrael damaged him or lost his money and is liable to pay by law.
who seized the field. Held it by force.
for the buyer says to the owners, etc.. And it is proven from this that the gentile took from him lawfully.
in their courts. In the courts of the gentiles, for the gentile cannot evade the law.
if the owners have the means. If they have enough money and want to buy it.
they have precedence over everyone. And another person cannot buy it.

a quarter of the land or a third of the money, etc.. Since we assume that the buyer paid only three-quarters of the true value of the land, he must give the owners a third of what he paid, which is what he saved, or a quarter of the land, since he paid only for three-quarters of its value.

therefore the buyer from the oppressor for thirty gives the owners ten. Since the gentile discounts by about a quarter, presumably it is worth about forty, and the oppressor discounted it by about ten.
that is suited for planting. More suitable for planting than for sowing (Rashi, Bava Metzia 101a).
we estimate how much a person would be willing to give for planting this field. How much he would pay someone to plant it for him, which is generally a sum between the expense and the improvement.
we assess for him and his hand is on the lower. We estimate the investment and the value of the improvement, and he is paid the lesser of the two.
we listen to him. And he need not pay at all the person who went down into his field.
which exhausts. Depletes the soil, because the trees reduce its strength.
and upper rooms. Structures on the roof of the house.
one who goes down into his fellow's field with permission, etc.. That he gave him permission to work the field, but the one who went down planted in a field not meant for planting.

and a husband in his wife's property, etc.. The commentators struggled with which property is meant here, since the wife's property generally mentioned is property in which the husband's status is not that of one who goes down with permission (see Hilchot Ishut 23:8-9). Therefore they wrote that this refers to unusual situations of a minor who exercised refusal (Maggid Mishneh, based on Hilchot Ishut there halakhah 10), or to property given to the wife on condition that her husband have no right in it (Bach; and see Yad Peshutah, who explained differently).
and a partner in a field in which he has a share is like one who goes down with permission. For he has permission to work the joint property.
we assess for him and his hand is on the upper. The hand of the one who went down, as with one who goes down with permission.
his ruin. A ruined structure.
my wood and my stones. The building materials.
because it exhausts the land. As above halakhah 5, and see Even HaAzel, who discusses what kind of exhausting of land applies here.
that he swear while holding an object. While holding a Torah scroll in his hand.
how much he spent. Because the expense is not visible, whereas the improvement is visible and not subject to dispute.
and if he said, etc.. The one who went down can say that he prefers not to swear but that the judges assess his expense according to the low market estimate.
he does not need an oath. Because it is visible and can be estimated.
and he swears a heset oath. See above 4:4 in the commentary.
for the land is presumed to belong to its owner. And the improvement is also in his possession, and the one who went down comes to take money from him and must bring proof.
a husband who sent down, etc.. See also Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 8:6.
sharecroppers. Workers who work the field for a share of the crop.
in his wife's property. Usufruct property, whose substance belongs to the wife while the husband is entitled to its produce.

and afterward he divorced her. And the law is that the land returns to the wife (and this speaks of a case where he has not yet eaten of the produce, in which case she pays him as one who went down without permission; if he did eat of the produce, she pays him nothing, and not the sharecroppers either, Beit Shmuel, Even HaEzer 88, subsection 22).

if the husband himself was a sharecropper... for they went down to it only with the husband's consent. As sub-sharecroppers, and they agreed that they would not receive more than the husband receives.
and if the husband is not a sharecropper, they went down on the field's account. And the husband's law is like that of anyone who hires sharecroppers.
and we assess for them as a sharecropper. Who is entitled to a share of the produce. And the husband must pay them their value, since he sent them down (Tur, Even HaEzer 88).
and one who sees a lost item of a Yisrael and ignores it and leaves it, etc.. See further below 14:7.
took the lost item and did not return it, etc.. See below 14:6.
and violates "you shall not steal". See below 14:7, that he violates this prohibition only if he took it for himself before its owners despaired of it.
for appetite. For his enjoyment.

but one who eats carrion to spite is a heretic. If he became accustomed to transgress to spite, he is an apostate and is regarded as denying the commandments of the Torah (Hilchot Teshuvah 3:9; and "heretic" here is used in the general sense of all kinds of denial, Yad Peshutah).
and the heretics among Israel and the epicureans. See Hilchot Teshuvah 3:7-8.
and idol worshippers and public desecrators of Shabbat. See Hilchot Shabbat 30:15.
publicly. In front of ten Jews (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 12:4).
for it is said. Regarding the commandment of returning a lost item.
trustworthy people. Reliable people.
and everywhere. Even if in that place there is no desecration of God's name if he does not return his lost item.
bring in their vessels. To a place where they will be kept safe.
and erred. In favor of the Yisrael.
to test him. To examine his trustworthiness.
he takes and announces. Perhaps the lost item belongs to a Yisrael.
and gave its identifying marks. See below 13:1-3.
in a main road. A principal thoroughfare.
and a plaza. A broad area where people come to trade.

in synagogues and study halls. For example, where there were synagogues or study halls outside the city guarded by gentiles (Rashi, Bava Metzia 24a). And although the gentiles are not the majority there, since they stay in the place while the Israelites merely pass by, it is reasonable that the gentiles would find the lost item (Ritva, ibid.).

for he despaired of it when it fell. Since the loser despaired, the finder acquired the lost item, and therefore he is not obligated to return it to the loser even when he gives its identifying marks.
one who wishes to go in the way of the good and the upright. See also below halakhah 17.
returns the lost item to a Yisrael, etc.. Even though he despaired of it.
its wine is forbidden for benefit. Because ordinary gentile wine is forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 11:3).
and its jug is permitted on account of lost property. The jug belongs to the finder and may be used after it is made fit (see ibid. halakhah 15).

and if a Yisrael came and gave its identifying marks, it is permitted to drink to the one who found it. Since it became clear that this is a Yisrael's wine, it is permitted to drink, and he need not return it to the loser, since presumably he despaired of it.
this is permitted on account of lost property. But the meat is forbidden to eat, like meat that disappeared from sight (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 8:12).
in the depths of the sea. The sea bottom.
and in the current of a river that does not cease. The flow of a river that does not dry up.
and it is found. It is commonly found.
for he certainly despaired of it. Since it cannot be rescued from there.
we do not attend to him. We do not help in returning his property.
in a stall that has no opening. That has no door.
his purse. A wallet with coins in it.
and although it is forbidden for one who sees this to take it for himself. Because failure to guard his property does not show that he abandoned it (Beit Yosef).
to attend to it. To take care of it.
a basket. A basket.

if he was a sage or an elder of honor... he is not obligated to attend to them. So the Sages taught from the words "and you hide yourself from them," meaning that sometimes one ignores the lost item (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 30a, and see Hilchot Kilayim 10:29; and see Hilchot Rotzeach UShemirat HaNefesh 13:3-4, a similar law regarding the commandment of unloading and loading).
in the field. Where there are not many people, and he forgoes his honor.
if he found them in the field he must return them until they reach the owners' domain. Even if they are in the city.
(. And the reason is explained below, halakhah 14.
and struck it. Hit it and it went.

for he began the commandment. And since he began, he must finish the commandment (see Yad Peshutah and Aruch HaShulchan 263:2). Some explained that the reason is that he became like a guardian of the lost item and therefore bears responsibility for it until he returns it (see Chiddushei HaPele'ah on Shulchan Aruch 263:2).

he is liable for its responsibility. Like a guardian who did not return the deposit to its owner, who is liable for it. For a guardian of a lost item is like a paid guardian, who is liable if the item is lost (below 13:10).

but with living creatures, etc.. With animals it does not suffice to return them to a place where they will be seen in the near future, because they became accustomed to other paths when they were lost and may go away from there before they are seen. [Note: in some manuscripts, before the words "but with living creatures" the words were added: "In what case is this said? With an item that has no life."]
he has fulfilled the commandment. Since a sheepfold is a guarded place (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 31a).
a kohen who saw a lost item, etc.. See also Hilchot Rotzeach 13:3.
in a cemetery. And if he enters there he will be impure (Hilchot Evel 3:4).

a positive commandment of "they shall be holy". A positive commandment that the kohanim be set apart, holy, and prepared for the Temple service (see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:1). And when they are impure they cannot serve in the Temple (see Yad Peshutah).
the negative commandment of "he shall not defile himself as a husband among his people". For a kohen is forbidden to become defiled to the dead (Hilchot Evel 3:1).
and a positive commandment. Of returning a lost item.

and a positive commandment does not override a negative commandment together with a positive commandment. And although with a lost item there is also a negative commandment, nevertheless since it is the one that comes to override the prohibition of impurity, and does so by virtue of its positive commandment, we do not take into account the negative commandment in it (Rif, Bava Metzia 16b in the pages of the Rif).
and he should not accept from him. He should not accept and act according to his words.

for if he accepted from his father, etc.. And the positive commandment of honoring parents does not override the positive and negative commandment involved in returning a lost item (and see Hilchot Mamrim 6:12 that honoring parents does not override any commandment).
and to prevent them. From spoiling.
to include the loss of his land. That preventing damage is also within the commandment of returning a lost item.
and encountered. Met.
equal to his teacher. In the wisdom of Torah.

his teacher's takes precedence. For his teacher takes precedence over his father in matters of honor, "for his father brought him into this world, and his teacher who taught him wisdom brings him to the life of the World to Come" (Hilchot Talmud Torah 5:1, where it says that if his father is a sage his lost item takes precedence even if he is not equal to his teacher; and see the commentary and Piskei VeShitot there for an explanation of the matter).

and even though his donkey came up on its own, etc.. Even if the rescuer's donkey was saved from the water on its own and it turns out the rescuer lost nothing, since the condition for payment was that he rescue his fellow's donkey and leave his own, and so he did, he receives the sum stipulated. And the fact that his donkey was saved is unrelated to the condition; rather Heaven had mercy on him so that he would not lose his donkey (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 116a).
worth. Worth.
a maneh. A hundred dinars.

he has only his fitting wage. The wage for the effort of saving the donkey, and not the value of his donkey that he lost (and below in halakhah 4 it is explained what the law is if he stopped his work and lost its wage).
the value of mine. The value of his donkey, worth a maneh.
or he stipulated before the court. That he take the value of his donkey, and the owners or the court agreed to this (below halakhah 4).

he went down to save and did not save, he has only his fitting wage. And he does not take the value of his donkey, because payment of the value of his donkey is conditional on his saving his fellow's donkey (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 116b).

rather he gives him his wage as an idle worker who is idle from the work he was engaged in. We estimate how much he usually receives for his work and how much he would be willing to reduce from that wage in order to rest and be idle from his work, and this sum depends on the amount of effort and exertion in his usual work (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 4:6).
his own takes precedence. For the loss of a wage has the law of a lost item, and his lost item takes precedence over anyone else's.
this one with a barrel of wine and that one with a jar of honey. And honey is more valuable than wine.
and anyone who saves, saves for himself. And he need not give the honey to its original owners.
hin. Yes.
he jested with him. He mocked him.
a ferry. A vessel for crossing between the two banks of a river.
he has only his fitting wage. Because he mocked him.
a fisherman. A fisher.
and said to him, cancel your net and take me across. He asked him to give up fishing in order to take him across, and he agreed.
he gives him what he stipulated with him. As explained above in halakhah 3.
and a troop stood over it and plundered it. Soldiers came upon it and captured it.
if they cannot save from their hands. Their property.
and one of them stood up and saved. Part of their property, or all of it.
he saved for himself. For he is regarded as acquiring from ownerless property.
saves for the middle. For all of them (see Piskei VeShitot).
with difficulty. With great effort.
anyone who saves, saves for the middle. As in the case where they could have saved, above halakhah 8.
there were two partners. And they went with the joint property.

and one of them saved, he saved for the middle. Whether it was possible to save or it was not possible to save (Maggid Mishneh). For since they are partners, presumably he saved for both, unless he announced that he is saving only for himself.
he has separated himself from his fellow. He separated himself from his partner.
he has retracted from the hire. For a worker may retract in the middle of the work (Hilchot Sechirut 9:4).
